message: Your latest mood entry is low, and your recent mood trend is down.
action: Consider reaching out to someone you trust. For crisis support in the US and its territories, call or text 988. Elsewhere, contact your local crisis service; for immediate danger, call local emergency services.
why: Your latest mood rating and recent trend prompted this check-in. These entries cannot assess your safety or explain how you feel.

message: Your recent mood trend is down.
action: If it feels right, send a message to someone you trust or add a note about today.
why: A recent downward trend is worth noticing. It does not explain the reason for the change.

message: Your latest entries show lower mood alongside less than six recorded hours of sleep.
action: Review your sleep entry and note how you feel today.
why: These sleep and mood entries appear together. They do not measure brain chemistry or establish a cause.

message: The middle of your recorded sleep period differs by more than 90 minutes from your comparison pattern.
action: Review your recent bedtimes and wake times, and check that the entries are accurate.
why: A change in recorded sleep timing does not establish a change in your body clock or predict when you will feel sleepy.

message: Your latest step count is below 2,000, alongside a lower mood entry.
action: If movement feels suitable for you, consider a short, comfortable activity.
why: Step counts and mood ratings give context together. They do not show why your mood or energy changed.

message: Your latest sleep entry exceeds nine and a half hours, and mood is below your recorded baseline.
action: Check the sleep entry and add a note about how you felt on waking.
why: Sleep duration and mood alone do not measure grogginess, sleep stage at waking or recovery.

message: Your mood trend is down, with no social tag recorded for more than four days.
action: If you would like some company, send a brief check-in to someone you trust.
why: Social tags record what you choose to log. A gap does not mean you have been isolated.

message: You logged stress alongside less than six hours of sleep.
action: If it feels comfortable, try a brief breathing practice at your own pace.
why: The stressed tag and sleep entry prompted this suggestion. They do not measure nervous-system activity.

message: At least 95% of scheduled doses are recorded as taken over the past seven days.
action: Review your medication log and keep reminders aligned with your medication instructions.
why: This percentage summarizes dose records. It does not measure how well a medicine is working.

message: Some scheduled doses are not recorded as taken over the past seven days.
action: Review the log for missing or incorrect entries. Ask your pharmacist if medication timing is difficult.
why: The log cannot tell whether a missing entry reflects a missed dose or what made logging difficult.

message: Fewer than 70% of scheduled doses are recorded as taken over the past seven days.
action: Review the log. For questions about missed doses or timing, check your medication instructions or ask your pharmacist.
why: Dose records may be incomplete. Reclaim cannot choose your next dose or change your schedule.

message: Your latest mood entry is on the low end of the scale.
action: If you want to, add a sentence about what has been happening around you.
why: A note can preserve context for you to revisit. A rating alone does not explain how you feel.

message: Your latest mood entry is below your recorded baseline.
action: Consider noting what feels different today or what support you would like.
why: Your baseline compares your own entries. A difference does not identify a hidden burden or its cause.

message: Your latest mood entry is above your recorded baseline.
action: If you want to, add a tag or note about today.
why: Context beside a higher rating gives you something to reflect on later without deciding what caused it.

message: Your recent mood trend is down.
action: Consider making space for an activity you find restful, or reaching out for support.
why: The trend summarizes recent entries. It cannot establish recovery debt or predict tomorrow's mood.

message: Your mood trend is down and you have logged a stressed tag.
action: If a task feels manageable, choose one small step to try.
why: These entries show stress alongside a mood change. They do not measure dopamine or explain motivation.

message: Your recent mood trend is up.
action: Note something you would like to keep doing, if it still suits you.
why: A rising trend describes your entries. It cannot show which habit made the difference.

message: Your recent entries include a stress flag.
action: If you would like a pause, try a comfortable breathing practice.
why: This suggestion follows the recorded stress flag. You can choose whether a breathing practice feels helpful.

message: No tags yet — tags are how insights become personal instead of generic.
action: Next check-in: add one tag (stressed / calm / focused / social / training).
why: Tags add context alongside your mood rating and let Reclaim match tag-based prompts.

message: Your recorded seven-day sleep average is below six and a half hours.
action: Review the week's sleep entries and note anything you want to discuss or adjust with support.
why: This is an average of recorded sleep. It does not establish chronic sleep debt or your individual sleep needs.

message: Your latest entries show less than six hours of sleep alongside a higher mood rating.
action: Check how rested you feel and add any missing sleep details.
why: A higher mood rating does not tell us how a short sleep period affected you.

message: The middle of your recorded sleep period has shifted earlier by more than 90 minutes.
action: Review recent bedtimes and wake times and note any schedule changes.
why: An earlier recorded midpoint describes timing. It does not establish why the timing changed.

message: Your latest records show under six and a half hours of sleep and fewer than 2,500 steps.
action: If you feel like moving, choose an activity that is comfortable and suitable for you.
why: These records do not measure motivation or tell us why activity was lower.

message: Your mood trend is down and you logged feeling stressed.
action: Consider what support or pause would feel useful today.
why: A stressed tag adds context to the mood trend. These entries do not establish accumulating strain.

message: Lower medication logging and a below-baseline mood entry appear together.
action: Review the medication log; ask your pharmacist about any difficulty following your medication instructions.
why: These records do not establish whether mood affected medication use or whether medication affected mood.

message: You recorded a completed session today alongside a higher mood entry.
action: Note how you felt around the session, if you would like to.
why: A completed session and one mood rating do not establish a personal correlation or show what changed your mood.

message: It has been at least three days since a recorded session, and your latest mood entry is lower.
action: Review your training plan and how you feel before deciding on your next activity.
why: A gap between logged sessions does not tell us whether you needed rest or did other activity.

message: You recorded training today after less than six hours of sleep.
action: Review your session and how you felt. Discuss concerns about suitable training with a qualified professional.
why: These entries cannot determine a safe load adjustment or measure recovery.

message: It has been at least seven days since a recorded training session.
action: Review your plan and current circumstances before your next session.
why: A gap in the log does not show detraining, injury status or readiness to resume.

message: At least five sessions are recorded this week alongside a lower mood entry.
action: Review your recent sessions and note how you are feeling before planning more activity.
why: Session count and mood do not establish fatigue, overreaching or the amount of recovery you need.

message: One or fewer sessions are recorded this week, and your mood trend is down.
action: Review your training plan and choose a next step that suits your current circumstances.
why: These records describe session frequency and mood together. They do not show that training less explains the mood change.

message: At least three training sessions are recorded this week.
action: Log one thing you want to improve next week.
why: This count describes your logged sessions. It does not measure physical adaptation or prescribe a weekly target.

message: Your latest mood entry is higher, and the last recorded session was one to two days ago.
action: Review your next planned session when it suits you.
why: The gap is between logged sessions; it does not prove that today is a rest day or predict readiness.

message: You recorded at least two sessions this week and a sleep average of seven hours or more.
action: Review your training and sleep records together.
why: Session counts and sleep duration do not measure strength gains, recovery quality or hormone levels.

message: Your sleep entries are available to review.
action: Check your latest entry or add any missing sleep details.
why: Keeping sleep records gives you a history to look back on when reflecting on your routine.

message: Mood gets clearer when you capture context, not just a number.
action: If you want to, write one line about how you feel and what is happening around you.
why: A short note preserves context beside a mood rating for later reflection.

message: Your medication log is available to review.
action: Check that your records and reminders reflect your current medication instructions.
why: Logging records what you report. It does not set a dose, choose medication timing or assess effectiveness.

message: You can choose one small thing to focus on today.
action: If you would like to, note a manageable next step.
why: This is a general reflection prompt. It does not assess your energy or predict a change in mood.

message: Would a short pause feel useful?
action: Choose a comfortable breathing practice if you would like one.
why: This is an optional general prompt, not an assessment of your stress or nervous system.

message: Take a moment to notice how you are feeling.
action: If you want to, note anything you would like to attend to.
why: This is a general check-in. Reclaim has no hydration measurement for this prompt.

message: Your latest record shows sleep efficiency below 80% and duration below seven hours.
action: Review the sleep record and note any concerns to discuss with a qualified professional.
why: Recorded sleep efficiency describes the relationship between logged sleep and time in bed. It does not establish a sleep disorder or determine treatment.

message: Your tracker recorded less than 40 minutes of deep sleep in a sleep period of at least six hours.
action: Check the entry and note how rested you feel.
why: A sleep-stage estimate does not measure whether your physical recovery is complete.

message: Your tracker recorded less than an hour of REM sleep alongside a lower mood entry.
action: Review the sleep estimate and add any context you want to remember.
why: Sleep-stage estimates and mood ratings do not establish why you feel this way.

message: Your recorded sleep shortfall estimate is over six hours.
action: Review the entries and the sleep target used for this estimate.
why: A calculated shortfall depends on recorded sleep and the reference target. It does not measure cognitive impairment.

message: Your latest sleep quality score is lower, while your seven-day recorded sleep average is at least six and a half hours.
action: Review the sleep entry and note any disruptions you noticed.
why: A quality score and a weekly average do not establish last night's sleep stages or explain a disruption.

message: The middle of your recorded sleep period has shifted later by more than 90 minutes.
action: Review recent bedtimes and wake times and note any schedule changes.
why: A later recorded midpoint describes timing. It does not establish a body-clock disorder.

message: Your latest mood entry is more than one point below your recorded baseline.
action: Consider noting what feels different today or what support you would like.
why: Your baseline is a comparison with earlier entries. It cannot determine the cause or significance of a change.

message: Your latest sleep entry is more than an hour and a half below your recorded baseline.
action: Review the entry and note how rested you feel.
why: Your historical average is a reference for your records, not a measurement of your body's sleep requirement.

message: Your latest records show shorter sleep, a lower mood rating and fewer steps.
action: Review the entries together and consider what support would feel useful.
why: These three observations appear together. They do not establish depletion or explain how one affects another.

message: Lower medication logging and a downward mood trend appear together.
action: Review the medication log and keep reminders aligned with your medication instructions.
why: The records do not show whether doses were missed or whether medication and mood changes are connected.

message: You recorded training today, a higher mood entry and a weekly sleep average of at least seven hours.
action: Look back over your session and note how it felt.
why: These entries do not measure readiness for harder training or other demanding activities.

message: Your records include stress, shorter sleep and lower medication logging.
action: Review the entries and note any concerns you want to discuss with your care team.
why: These observations do not establish a shared cause or show which change would help you.

message: A medication you track has a sleep-related catalogue tag, alongside a shorter latest sleep entry.
action: Note sleep timing and medication logging together for a few days before drawing any conclusions.
why: Catalogue tags describe where a medication type may overlap with interpretation — they do not diagnose you or explain last night. Pairing sleep logs with med timing helps you and your clinician see patterns without assuming causation.

message: Mood has trended down while a mood-relevant medication is in your list — Reclaim treats that as overlapping context, not a treatment verdict.
action: Keep logging mood and doses; bring patterns to your clinician if they persist.
why: Medication type tags and mood telemetry can line up without implying the medication failed or succeeded. Context helps interpretation; decisions stay with your care team.

message: It has been more than five days since a recorded session, and a medication on your list has a training-related catalogue tag.
action: If readiness feels off, log how you felt before deciding whether to train — medication context is not a go/no-go rule.
why: Training-readiness catalogue tags describe where medication might matter in interpretation. They do not replace how your body feels or professional guidance about training load.

message: No social tag is recorded for more than four days, alongside a downward mood trend.
action: If you would like some connection, consider messaging someone you trust.
why: A gap in social tags is a gap in logging. It cannot establish isolation or explain the mood trend.

message: Your latest step count exceeds 8,000 and your recorded weekly sleep average is below seven hours.
action: Review your sleep history alongside your activity records.
why: Steps and sleep duration do not establish whether recovery is complete or whether training is suitable.

message: Your latest mood entry is higher and your recent trend is up.
action: If you want to, note what has been different recently.
why: Noticing what is associated with a positive mood trend can help you reflect on patterns. Your entries do not establish which factors made the difference.

message: Your latest mood entry is higher and your recent mood trend has risen.
action: If you want to, note what has been happening around you.
why: An upward trend does not establish a prior crisis, prove resilience or identify what made the difference.

message: Your latest records show at least seven and a half hours of sleep alongside a higher mood entry.
action: Note anything you would like to remember about the night.
why: Sleep duration and mood appear together here. They do not establish sleep quality or a cause of the mood rating.

message: The middle of your latest recorded sleep period differs by less than 30 minutes from your comparison pattern.
action: Review how your recent sleep timing has felt to you.
why: Your recorded sleep times have been similar recently. You can view how that pattern is associated with your daytime mood without assuming one explains the other.

message: Between 85% and 95% of scheduled doses are recorded as taken over the past seven days.
action: Review your medication log and keep reminders aligned with your medication instructions.
why: The percentage summarizes records; it does not measure therapeutic levels or treatment effectiveness.

message: Some scheduled doses are not logged this week.
action: If you missed a dose, check your medication instructions or ask your pharmacist what to do.
why: An unlogged dose does not confirm a missed dose. Reclaim cannot determine how you should handle a missed dose or change your medication schedule.

message: Your latest recorded step count exceeds 10,000.
action: Reflect on the activity if you would like to; your next activity can suit your current needs.
why: A step count describes recorded movement. It does not measure brain chemistry or establish a daily target.

message: Your latest recorded step count is below 1,500.
action: Check the record for missing activity. If you feel like moving, choose something suitable for you.
why: Step counts may not capture every type of movement. One count does not establish a sedentary streak or a neurochemical deficit.

message: Your recent entries include stress alongside at least seven recorded hours of sleep.
action: Try a 5-minute decompression window: no inputs, just breathing or staring out a window.
why: Sleep duration alone does not explain stress. These entries show parallel context; they cannot establish which factors are associated with how you feel.

message: At least three sessions are recorded this week, alongside a mood entry of three or higher.
action: Review your next planned session and check how you feel before starting.
why: These records summarize sessions and mood. They do not measure productivity, hormone levels or readiness.

message: At least six sessions are recorded this week, alongside shorter average sleep and a lower mood entry.
action: Review your plan and discuss persistent concerns with a qualified professional.
why: Session count, sleep duration and mood alone cannot diagnose overreaching or prescribe recovery.

message: At least four sessions are recorded this week, and your sleep shortfall estimate exceeds four hours.
action: Review your training and sleep records before discussing any plan changes.
why: These records do not determine whether you need a deload or how much your training should change.

message: Your latest sleep entry is below six and a half hours, while your weekly average is at least that long.
action: Check the entry and note how rested you feel today.
why: One shorter entry alongside a weekly average does not determine whether you need a nap or what timing would suit you.

message: Your latest mood entry is three or higher, and the recent trend has not fallen by more than 5%.
action: If you would like to, choose a small moment to check in with yourself tomorrow.
why: These entries are a snapshot of mood. They do not predict how a new habit will affect your day.

message: Some scheduled doses are not recorded as taken over the past seven days.
action: Review reminder settings against your medication instructions. Ask your pharmacist if timing or storage is unclear.
why: A logging percentage does not explain a habit or justify moving medication to a different time or storage location.

message: Your latest mood entry is lower, with no social tag recorded for more than six days.
action: If you would like some company, consider contacting someone you trust.
why: Missing social tags do not establish isolation or measure social connection.

message: Your recorded sleep midpoint differs by more than an hour, and the latest sleep entry is under seven hours.
action: Review your recent sleep timing and any changes in your schedule.
why: The timing difference does not establish a circadian delay or show why your sleep duration changed.

message: Your recent records include stress alongside more than 7,000 steps.
action: If you want to, note how you felt during the activity.
why: Movement and stress recorded together do not show that movement has changed your stress.

message: Your latest entries show a higher mood rating alongside less than six hours of sleep.
action: Review the sleep entry and note how rested you feel.
why: A higher mood rating and shorter sleep do not establish an adrenaline response or measure impairment.

message: You recorded a completed session today alongside a lower mood entry.
action: If you remember, note how you felt before and after the session.
why: A completed session and one mood entry do not show whether your mood changed during exercise.

message: Your sleep shortfall estimate is above three hours, with a weekly recorded average below seven and a half hours.
action: Review the sleep entries and note any concerns or schedule changes.
why: A calculated shortfall is not a prescription for a sleep-in or a measure of how quickly you can recover.

message: Your latest mood entry is lower, with fewer than two context tags.
action: If you would like to, add a tag or note about what is on your mind.
why: A tag adds context to the rating and can help Reclaim match relevant prompts.

message: Your latest step count is between 3,000 and 6,000, alongside a mood entry of three or higher.
action: Review your activity and choose any next step around your own circumstances and guidance.
why: These entries do not establish readiness to increase activity or determine an appropriate increase.

message: Fewer than half of scheduled doses are recorded as taken over the past seven days.
action: Review the log. If you are having difficulty following medication instructions, talk with your pharmacist or prescriber.
why: A missing record does not confirm a missed dose. This percentage cannot assess treatment effect or identify a barrier.

message: Your latest recorded sleep efficiency is at least 90%.
action: If you want to, note how rested you felt when you woke.
why: The recorded ratio of sleep to time in bed does not establish sleep-stage quality or how restorative the night was.

message: Your latest mood entry is three, with a small downward trend.
action: If a task feels manageable, consider trying one small step.
why: The entries describe a small mood change. They do not predict whether starting a task will change how you feel.

message: Your latest records show at least seven and a half hours of sleep, a higher mood entry and at least 7,000 steps.
action: Check how you feel and what, if anything, you would like to focus on today.
why: These are three recorded observations. They do not measure full recovery or readiness for demanding activity.

message: Your latest recorded step count is more than 1,000 above your baseline.
action: If you want to, note what was different about that activity.
why: Your baseline compares recorded step counts. It does not establish an activity target or measure mood benefits.

message: A social tag was recorded recently, alongside a higher mood entry.
action: If you want to, note how that interaction felt.
why: A social tag and a mood rating do not establish what affected your mood.

message: Your finished workouts this week include active energy from your connected health data — useful context alongside sets and reps.
action: End sessions from the workout flow when you can so each session can line up the best time window for calories.
why: Active calories estimate exertion during a time window. Pairing them with training logs makes weekly load easier to read without reducing workouts to one number.

message: Your last sleep includes overnight SpO₂ and breathing rate from your tracker — use them as context with sleep length, not a diagnosis.
action: If something feels wrong physically, rely on proper clinical assessment rather than these estimates alone.
why: Consumer wearables approximate physiology. Showing them next to sleep duration helps you notice patterns while avoiding over-interpreting any single night.

message: Your connected-health resting heart-rate trend is above its recorded baseline, alongside a lower mood entry.
action: Review the records. If you feel unwell or are concerned, contact a healthcare professional.
why: These records describe a heart-rate trend and a mood entry. They do not identify a cause or diagnose illness.
